lead: The first law says energy is conserved. It does not say which way a process may go. The second law adds direction. It forbids a cyclic engine from turning heat from one reservoir completely into work, and forbids a refrigerator from moving heat from cold to hot without work input. These are the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements. They are equivalent. They explain why a power plant needs a condenser and why 100% thermal efficiency is impossible. This chapter states both forms and proves their equivalence by contradiction.
prereq: You need: the first law energy balance for a cyclic process, and the definitions of heat, work and a system from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A heat reservoir is a large body whose temperature stays constant when heat enters or leaves it. A river, the atmosphere or a large condenser can act as one over a short time. A cyclic device returns to its initial state after each cycle, so its internal energy change is zero. For an engine between a hot reservoir at T<sub>H</sub> and a cold reservoir at T<sub>C</sub>, let Q<sub>H</sub> be heat taken from the hot reservoir, Q<sub>C</sub> be heat rejected to the cold reservoir, and W be work delivered. Use positive magnitudes in kJ.

The first law for one cycle gives W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>. Thermal efficiency is the work obtained per unit heat supplied: η = W/Q<sub>H</sub>. η is a fraction; multiply by 100 for percent. The first law allows Q<sub>C</sub> = 0, so η = 100%. The second law forbids that case.
W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>,   η = W/Q<sub>H</sub> = (Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>)/Q<sub>H</sub>
blocks.where: Q<sub>H</sub> is heat taken from the hot reservoir (kJ); Q<sub>C</sub> is heat rejected to the cold reservoir (kJ); W is work delivered per cycle (kJ); η is thermal efficiency (dimensionless).

blocks.text: Engine, refrigerator and heat-pump hardware is in 3.2.

Kelvin–Planck statement: no cyclic device can take heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work. It may take Q<sub>H</sub> from a hot reservoir, but it must reject some heat Q<sub>C</sub> > 0 to a colder reservoir. Therefore W < Q<sub>H</sub> and η < 1. Some syllabi call this the Kelvin–Planck statement. The word cyclic matters. A single expansion of gas can produce work while cooling; it is not a cycle. A device that claims to violate this statement is a perpetual motion machine of the second kind, PMM2. It does not violate the first law; it takes heat from air or sea and produces work forever in a cycle. The statement says PMM2 is impossible. Work can become heat fully: a paddle wheel stirred in water converts work into internal energy. The restriction is one-way.

Clausius statement: no cyclic device can move heat from a colder body to a hotter body without work input. A refrigerator takes QC from the cold space, receives work Win, and rejects QH = QC + Win to the warm surroundings. Its coefficient of performance is COPR = QC/Win. A heat pump has COPHP = QH/Win = COPR + 1. COP can be greater than 1; it is not efficiency. COP = 5 means 5 kJ of cold-side heat removed per 1 kJ of work. The statement applies to the net effect of a complete cycle, not to a single process. It forbids COPR = ∞ for a cyclic refrigerator with no work. Practical cycles are in 3.9.

blocks.where: Q<sub>C</sub> is heat removed from the cold space (kJ); Q<sub>H</sub> is heat rejected to the warm space (kJ); W<sub>in</sub> is work input per cycle (kJ); COP<sub>R</sub> and COP<sub>HP</sub> are dimensionless coefficients of performance.

blocks.text: Kelvin–Planck and Clausius are equivalent: if one is false, the other is false. Suppose Kelvin–Planck is false. A cyclic engine E takes Q<sub>H</sub> from the hot reservoir and delivers W = Q<sub>H</sub>, rejecting no heat. Use W to drive a normal refrigerator R between the same reservoirs. R takes Q<sub>C</sub> from the cold reservoir and rejects Q<sub>C</sub> + W to the hot reservoir. Combine E and R. The hot reservoir loses Q<sub>H</sub> to E and gains Q<sub>C</sub> + Q<sub>H</sub> from R; net gain is Q<sub>C</sub>. The cold reservoir loses Q<sub>C</sub>. The composite moves Q<sub>C</sub> from cold to hot with no net work input, because E supplies W and R consumes W. That violates Clausius. So not-KP implies not-Clausius.

Now suppose Clausius is false. A device R moves Q<sub>C</sub> from the cold reservoir to the hot reservoir with no work input. Take a normal engine E that removes Q<sub>H</sub> from the hot reservoir, rejects Q<sub>C</sub> to the cold reservoir, and delivers W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>. The cold reservoir gains Q<sub>C</sub> from E and loses Q<sub>C</sub> to R; net change is zero. The hot reservoir loses Q<sub>H</sub> and gains Q<sub>C</sub>; net loss is Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub> = W. The composite takes heat W from the hot reservoir only and delivers work W in a cycle. That violates Kelvin–Planck. So not-Clausius implies not-KP. The two statements stand or fall together.

figure.caption: A real engine takes 100 kJ from the hot reservoir at 600 K, rejects 60 kJ to the cold reservoir at 300 K and delivers 40 kJ; the dashed perfect engine would reject 0 kJ and deliver 100 kJ, which the Kelvin–Planck statement forbids.

spec.title: Second-law statements
spec.aria: A real engine takes 100 kJ from a hot reservoir at 600 K, rejects 60 kJ to a cold reservoir at 300 K and delivers 40 kJ, while a dashed perfect engine would take the same 100 kJ and deliver all of it as work.

examples.question: A cyclic engine takes 100 kJ from a 600 K reservoir and rejects 60 kJ to a 300 K reservoir in each cycle. Find W and η. Does it violate the Kelvin–Planck statement?
steps: Data: Q<sub>H</sub> = 100 kJ, Q<sub>C</sub> = 60 kJ, T<sub>H</sub> = 600 K, T<sub>C</sub> = 300 K.
First law for one cycle: W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub> = 100 kJ − 60 kJ = 40 kJ.
Thermal efficiency: η = W/Q<sub>H</sub> = 40 kJ / 100 kJ = 0.40 = 40%.
Kelvin–Planck violation would require Q<sub>C</sub> = 0, so W = Q<sub>H</sub>. Here Q<sub>C</sub> = 60 kJ > 0 and W = 40 kJ < 100 kJ.
The engine is allowed by the Kelvin–Planck statement. The temperatures do not decide this point; they set the maximum possible η in 3.3.
examples.answer: W = 40 kJ and η = 40%; the engine does not violate the Kelvin–Planck statement because it rejects 60 kJ to the cold reservoir.
examples.check:
QH = 100.0
QC = 60.0
W = QH - QC
eta_percent = 100.0 * W / QH
print(W)
print(eta_percent)

traps: Thinking η = 100% is only inefficient. The first law allows it; the second law forbids it for a cyclic engine.
Applying Kelvin–Planck to a single process. It is a statement about a complete cycle; a gas can produce work while cooling in one expansion.
Treating COP > 1 as a violation. COP is heat moved per work input, not efficiency, so values like 4 are normal.
Confusing the two statements. Kelvin–Planck limits heat→work; Clausius limits cold→hot heat transfer without work.
Assuming Clausius says heat never flows cold to hot. It says a cyclic device cannot do so with no work input; a refrigerator does it with work.

quiz.a: No cyclic device can take heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work. It must reject some heat to a colder reservoir.
No cyclic device can move heat from a colder body to a hotter body without work input.

quiz.q: Why is a perpetual motion machine of the second kind not a first-law violation?
quiz.a: It conserves energy: it takes heat and produces equal work. It violates the second law because a cyclic device cannot convert heat from one reservoir completely into work.

quiz.q: A cyclic engine takes 500 kJ from a hot reservoir and rejects 300 kJ to a cold reservoir. Find W and η.
A refrigerator removes 120 kJ from a cold space using 30 kJ of work. Find its COP.
If the Kelvin–Planck statement were false, show how a combined device would violate the Clausius statement.
quiz.a: A perfect engine takes Q<sub>H</sub> and delivers W = Q<sub>H</sub>. Use W to drive a refrigerator that removes Q<sub>C</sub> from the cold reservoir and rejects Q<sub>C</sub> + W to the hot reservoir. Net hot gain is Q<sub>C</sub>, cold loss is Q<sub>C</sub>, and net work input is zero. This moves heat from cold to hot with no work, violating Clausius.

quiz.q: Why can COP be greater than 1 while η cannot?
quiz.a: For an engine, η = W/Q<sub>H</sub> and W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub>. Kelvin–Planck requires Q<sub>C</sub> > 0, so W < Q<sub>H</sub> and η < 1. For a refrigerator, COP<sub>R</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub>/W<sub>in</sub>; Q<sub>C</sub> can be much larger than W<sub>in</sub>, so COP<sub>R</sub> > 1 is allowed.

beyond: Not for the exam. These statements feed exergy analysis, which prices work lost by irreversibility in chemical plants. Chiller COP and heat-pump COP decide the operating cost of data centres and LNG terminals. Cryocoolers for MRI magnets and superconducting cables rely on the same cold-to-hot work requirement. Search: second-law efficiency, exergy, PMM2, coefficient of performance.
